entry: American musician and singer-songwriter. Raised mainly in [[Texas]], he lived much of his life in [[Portland, Oregon]]. After several years in the rock band Heatmiser, he began a solo career in 1994. His songs explore addiction and depression; "Miss Misery" was nominated for the 1998 Academy Award for Best Original Song. He died at his [[Los Angeles]] home at age 34, and the autopsy did not determine whether his two stab wounds were self-inflicted. His posthumous album *From a Basement on the Hill* was released in 2004.

Closed plane curve around two focal points, with a constant sum of distances to them. It generalizes a [[Circle|circle]], which is the case in which the two foci coincide. An ellipse's elongation is measured by its eccentricity, which ranges from 0 for a circle to 1 for the limiting case of a [[Parabola|parabola]]. Its area has a simple algebraic formula, but its exact perimeter requires integration. Ellipses are the closed type of [[Conic section|conic section]] and are common in physics and astronomy: the orbit of each planet in the [[Solar System]] is approximately an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. The name, from a Greek word meaning "omission," was given by [[Apollonius of Perga]].

Type of [[Galaxy|galaxy]] with a smooth, nearly featureless, ellipsoidal shape. [[Edwin Hubble]] classed it, with spiral and [[Lenticular galaxy|lenticular]] galaxies, as one of the three main classes of galaxy in his Hubble sequence. Most ellipticals are composed of older, low-mass [[Star|stars]], with a sparse [[Interstellar medium|interstellar medium]], so star formation is typically minimal. They make up about 10–15% of galaxies in the [[Virgo Supercluster]] and are preferentially found near the centers of galaxy clusters. Sizes range from dwarf ellipticals with tens of millions of stars to supergiants of over one hundred trillion. Every massive elliptical contains a [[Supermassive black hole|supermassive black hole]] at its center. Hubble had hypothesized that ellipticals evolved into spirals, a view later found to be false.

Island in New York Harbor, within the U.S. states of [[New Jersey]] and New York. It was the busiest immigrant inspection and processing station in the United States, where about 12 million immigrants were processed from 1892 to 1954. Its facilities were also used to detain prisoners of war in [[World War I]] and [[World War II]]. A 1998 Supreme Court ruling placed most of the island in New Jersey, and it has been part of the [[Statue of Liberty]] National Monument since 1965.

Deciduous and semi-deciduous tree of the genus *Ulmus*, in the family Ulmaceae. Elms are distributed over most of the Northern Hemisphere and are components of many natural [[Forest|forests]]. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, many [[Species|species]] and [[Cultivar|cultivars]] were planted as ornamental street and park trees in [[Europe]], North America and [[Australasia]]. Most mature elms of European or North American origin have since died from Dutch elm disease, a microfungus spread by [[Beetle|bark beetles]]. Disease-resistant cultivars have been developed to restore elms to forestry and landscaping. There are about 30 to 40 species, a number that is uncertain because of frequent hybridization, and the greatest diversity is in Asia. The American elm can exceed 30 meters (98 feet) in height. The fruit is a winged samara flushed with [[Chlorophyll|chlorophyll]], which allows photosynthesis before the leaves emerge.

Method for calculating the relative skill levels of players, originally devised for rating chess players. A player rated 100 points above an opponent is expected to score 64%, and rating points transfer from loser to winner after each game, making the system self-correcting. Ratings are comparative only and valid within their own pool. The system, created by Hungarian-American chess master Arpad Elo, has been adapted for [[Tennis|tennis]], [[Association football|association football]], [[Baseball|baseball]], [[Basketball|basketball]] and other [[Zero-sum game|zero-sum games]].

South African-born Canadian-American industrialist. Born in [[Pretoria]], South Africa, Musk emigrated to Canada in 1989 and became a U.S. citizen in 2002. He co-founded the web software company Zip2 in 1995, and X.com, which merged with Confinity to form [[PayPal]]. He founded [[SpaceX]] in 2002 and later became chief executive of Tesla. He also co-founded Neuralink and founded The Boring Company, and in 2022 he acquired Twitter, which he renamed [[X (social network)|X]]. Musk is a polarizing figure. Critics cite false or misleading statements and promotion of conspiracy theories, while supporters credit his companies with substantial reductions in launch costs and scaled electric-vehicle production. He was the largest donor in the 2024 U.S. presidential election, supporting [[Donald Trump]], and served as a senior adviser to Trump from January to May 2025.

British singer, songwriter and pianist. Known for his songwriting partnership with lyricist Bernie Taupin, he has sold over 300 million records. He has won five [[Grammy Awards]] and two [[Academy Awards]], and was knighted in 1998. He established the Elton John [[HIV/AIDS|AIDS]] Foundation in 1992. His tribute single to [[Diana, Princess of Wales]], "Candle in the Wind 1997," is the best-selling chart single of all time.

American singer and actor known as the "King of Rock and Roll." Born in Tupelo, Mississippi, Presley moved with his family to [[Memphis, Tennessee]] when he was 13. He began recording for Sun Records in 1954, and his blend of [[Country music|country]] music and [[Rhythm and blues|rhythm and blues]] made him the leading figure of rock and roll. Many at the time considered his performances a threat to the moral well-being of white American youth. RCA Victor sold ten million of his singles within a year. After devoting much of the 1960s to Hollywood films, he returned to the stage in 1968 with an [[NBC]] television special, followed by a long [[Las Vegas]] residency. Presley is among the best-selling music artists in history, with an estimated 500 million records sold, and [[Rolling Stone]] ranked him third among its 100 Greatest Artists. Years of substance abuse and unhealthy eating compromised his health.

Method of transmitting and receiving digital messages using electronic devices over a [[Computer network|computer network]]. Email uses a store-and-forward model, so neither sender nor recipient must be online at the same time. It operates primarily over the [[Internet]] and also over local area networks. Originally a text-only [[ASCII]] medium, Internet email was extended by MIME to carry other character sets and images. The first [[ARPANET]] network mail was sent in 1971, introducing the "@" symbol in addresses. Email is also a vector for [[Phishing|phishing]] and [[Malware|malware]], which has necessitated ongoing protocol enhancements.

Self-conscious [[Emotion|emotion]] of mild to severe discomfort, usually involving a perceived loss of [[Dignity|dignity]]. It is typically felt when someone commits, or thinks of committing, a socially unacceptable act that is witnessed by or revealed to others. Frequently grouped with [[Shame|shame]] and [[Guilt (emotion)|guilt]], embarrassment can have a profoundly negative effect on thoughts and behavior. Causes include being caught in a lie, unwanted attention to private matters, and being made the focus of attention. Embarrassment is usually accompanied by blushing, sweating, nervousness and fidgeting, and may bring feelings of [[Anger|anger]]. The idea that embarrassment serves an appeasing function originated with Goffman, who argued that the embarrassed person shows he or she is disturbed by the act. Adolescent boys who displayed more embarrassment were less likely to engage in aggressive or delinquent behavior.

Series of narrow-body, twin-engined regional jet airliners built by Brazilian [[Aerospace manufacturer|aerospace manufacturer]] Embraer. Designed to complement the earlier ERJ family, the E-Jets carry 66 to 124 passengers. The first E170 was delivered to LOT Polish Airlines in 2004, followed by larger E190 and E195 variants later that year. The first generation is powered by [[General Electric]] CF34 [[Turbofan|turbofan]] engines. The second-generation E2 family, introduced in the 2010s, uses more fuel-efficient engines.

Art of decorating fabric or other materials by using a needle to stitch [[Thread (textiles)|thread]] or [[Yarn|yarn]]. One of the oldest forms of needlework, embroidery developed from [[Sewing|sewing]] techniques used to mend and reinforce cloth. The earliest surviving embroidered cloth comes from Egypt, and works in [[China]] date to the [[Warring States period]] (5th–3rd century BC). Embroidery is used to embellish garments, quilts and accessories, and may incorporate [[Pearl|pearls]], beads or sequins. It is classified as free or surface work, counted-thread work such as cross-stitch, or canvas work. Today it serves decorative, functional and cultural purposes.

Initial stage of development of a multicellular [[Organism|organism]], beginning after fertilization. In sexually reproducing organisms, embryonic development begins when an [[Egg cell|egg cell]] is fertilized by a [[Sperm|sperm]] cell to form a single-celled zygote. The zygote divides into a blastula, which in [[Mammal|mammals]] is called a blastocyst and hatches before implanting in the womb. Gastrulation forms the three germ layers, neurulation forms the [[Nervous system|nervous system]], and organogenesis forms the tissues and organs. Plant embryos develop within a [[Seed|seed]]. A human embryo becomes a [[Fetus|fetus]] at the ninth week after conception.

Green [[Gemstone|gemstone]], a variety of the mineral [[Beryl|beryl]]. Trace amounts of [[Chromium|chromium]] or sometimes vanadium give it color, and it has a hardness of 7.5–8 on the [[Mohs scale]]. Most emeralds have many inclusions, so their toughness is classified as poor. Emerald is one of the traditional "big four" precious gems, along with [[Diamond|diamonds]], rubies and [[Sapphire|sapphires]]. Most emeralds are oiled to fill surface-reaching cracks, which improves clarity and stability. The finest stones have a vivid green hue and a medium to dark tone. Major sources include the mines of [[Colombia]] and [[Zambia]]. The name derives from the Greek *smaragdos*, meaning "green stone."

Medical treatment facility, usually within a [[Hospital|hospital]], specializing in emergency medicine. Known as an emergency room (ER) in the [[United States]] and accident and emergency (A&E) in the [[United Kingdom]], it treats patients who arrive without appointments, either by their own means or by [[Ambulance|ambulance]]. Because it must treat a broad range of illnesses and injuries, some life-threatening, staffing levels may vary with patient volume, although most departments operate 24 hours a day. Patients are prioritized through triage, a brief assessment that includes vital signs and a chief complaint. Those with evidently serious conditions, such as cardiac arrest, bypass triage. The world's first specialized trauma care center opened in 1911 at the University of Louisville Hospital in [[Louisville, Kentucky]].

Systematic reduction of a community's vulnerability to natural and human-made hazards, with coordinated response to disasters. Emergency management focuses on destructive events that overwhelm a community's own capacity, such as hurricanes, [[Pandemic|pandemics]] and [[Terrorism|terrorism]]. Its activities are generally grouped into preparedness, response, mitigation and recovery, and it requires collaboration among individuals, households, [[Non-governmental organization|non-governmental organizations]] and local, provincial and federal governments. Professional work includes search and rescue, providing for basic needs, and issuing evacuation alerts. Cleanup after [[Flood|floods]] exposes workers to hidden debris and a risk of [[Hypothermia|hypothermia]], so employers must minimize exposure, including through [[Personal protective equipment|personal protective equipment]].

Services providing urgent pre-hospital treatment and transport to definitive care for serious illness and injury. Also known as ambulance services, EMS is typically summoned by telephone to a dispatch center, which sends [[Ambulance|ambulances]], squad cars, motorcycles, boats or aircraft. Crews begin care on arrival at the scene and transport patients to the next point of care, usually a hospital's [[Emergency department|emergency department]]. Training varies widely; in English-speaking countries, staff are known as emergency medical technicians (EMTs) or paramedics. The first specialized battlefield ambulances were designed by Dominique Jean Larrey, chief surgeon to [[Napoleon|Napoleon Bonaparte]], whose horse-drawn wagons evacuated wounded soldiers. During the Middle Ages, the [[Knights Hospitaller]] also assisted wounded soldiers on the battlefield.

Act of permanently leaving one's country to settle elsewhere, the counterpart of [[Immigration|immigration]]. A migrant emigrates from one country and immigrates to another. Demographers distinguish push factors, such as poor living conditions, lack of employment, persecution and [[Famine|famine]], from pull factors, such as higher wages, educational opportunity and political freedom. Forced displacement, including through ethnic cleansing, makes [[Refugee|refugees]] and asylum seekers among the most marginalized migrants. Millions fled poverty and political turmoil in Europe for the Americas and Oceania in the 18th to 20th centuries, and millions left South China in the [[Diaspora|Chinese diaspora]] during the 19th and early 20th centuries. Some scholars criticize the push-pull approach, noting that similar lists could be compiled for places where no migration took place.

German-born American inventor and businessman. He invented the lateral-cut flat disc record, known as the gramophone record, and founded the United States Gramophone Company. An improved telephone transmitter he developed was one of the first [[Microphone|microphones]]; [[Thomas Edison|Edison]] contested the patent, and a 1901 appeals court declared it void and awarded Edison full rights. After 1883 he worked as a private researcher in [[Washington, D.C.]] He also developed a rotary engine and an early [[Helicopter|helicopter]], which he and his son Henry demonstrated for the U.S. Navy in 1922.

English actress. Known for playing Daenerys Targaryen in the [[HBO]] fantasy series [[Game of Thrones]], for which she received four Primetime Emmy Award nominations. She has also starred in films including *Me Before You* (2016) and *Solo: A Star Wars Story* (2018). She survived two subarachnoid hemorrhages caused by brain [[Aneurysm|aneurysms]] in 2011 and 2013, and later co-founded the charity SameYou to support neurorehabilitation for brain-injury survivors.

Administrative region of northern [[Italy]], with its capital at [[Bologna]]. One of the wealthiest and most developed regions in Europe, with the third highest gross domestic product per capita in Italy. It is home to the [[University of Bologna]], the oldest university in the world, and several [[UNESCO]] World Heritage cities, including [[Ravenna]]. It is a center of food and automobile production, including [[Ferrari]]. The region's name derives from the Via Aemilia, a Roman road completed in 187 BC.

Mexican revolutionary and guerrilla leader. A leading figure in the [[Mexican Revolution]] and the main leader of the people's revolution in the state of Morelos, he inspired the agrarian movement known as Zapatismo. Under dictator [[Porfirio Díaz]], landowners monopolized land and water in Morelos for [[Sugarcane|sugarcane]] production, and peasant communities faced increasing repression. His Plan of Ayala, issued in November 1911, called for land reform and the redistribution of land to peasants. Zapata's forces helped bring about the fall of Díaz, and in 1914 they briefly occupied [[Mexico City]] alongside [[Pancho Villa]]. Zapata refused to recognize the authority of Venustiano Carranza and was killed in an ambush. Zapatista generals later helped drive Carranza from power, and Article 27 of the 1917 Mexican Constitution was drafted in response to his agrarian demands.

English novelist and poet. Her only novel, *Wuthering Heights* (1847), was published under the pseudonym Ellis Bell and was criticized by many reviewers as coarse and immoral. It is now considered a classic of English literature. She co-wrote a book of poetry with her sisters [[Charlotte Brontë|Charlotte]] and Anne, and spent most of her life at home in Haworth, Yorkshire.

American poet. Born in Amherst, Massachusetts, into a prominent family, Dickinson wrote nearly 1,800 poems, of which only 10 were published during her lifetime. Her verse uses short, acerbic lines and slant rhyme, and deals primarily with nature and mortality. Few in her circle knew of her writing until after her death, when her sister Lavinia found the poems. The first selection, published in 1890 and edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd, was significantly altered to fit the poetic conventions of the time. Not until 1955 did Thomas H. Johnson compile a complete collection that restored the poems closer to her intentions. Some scholars believe censorship obscured the nature of her relationship with her sister-in-law Susan Huntington Gilbert Dickinson, which has been interpreted as romantic.
